title: Javali and the More Rivalry
subtitle: Valley of Shadows: Shivaji, Chandrarao More, and the Road to the Sea
region: Javali valley near Mahabaleshwar, Wai and the Ghats-Konkan passes
moral: Politics is often closest and hardest among rivals who share the same world.

sources.citation: Sabhasad Bakhar, tr. S.N. Sen, account of Javali and Chandrarao More
sources.note: Maratha narrative; the outcome is clear but the manner of More's death is disputed.

sources.citation: Stewart N. Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818, pp. 66-70
sources.note: Critical account of intra-Maratha rivalry under Bijapur.

sources.citation: Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan, 1300-1761, Cambridge University Press, 2005, ch. 7
sources.note: Non-communal Deccan context for mobile service elites and political competition.

sources.citation: G.S. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas, Vol. 1, 1946, pp. 70-75

panels.shot: wide, mist-wreathed aerial view of steep forested gorge and forts, Shivaji in foreground looking toward the unseen sea

dialogue.text: Before Shivaji challenged empires, he fought a Maratha rival for a shadowed valley whose passes to the sea would change the Deccan.

panels.shot: slow push-in over map-like view of western Deccan, from Pune plateau to Konkan coast

dialogue.text: In 1656, a young jagirdar in the hills and a seasoned sardar in a ravine wrestled over a question older than both: who would control the roads between plateau and sea?

panels.shot: medium shot inside hill fort courtyard, low angle on Shivaji among armed followers

dialogue.text: Shivaji, son of Shahaji, held scattered forts for the sultan of Bijapur, yet dreamed in quiet of a Swarajya of his own amid the broken hills.

panels.shot: wide establishing shot of Javali valley and Vishalgad-like fort perched over a gorge

dialogue.text: To his southwest lay Javali, a deep, forested valley of mist and ambush, crowned with strongholds and opening secret passes down to the Konkan coast.

panels.shot: medium shot of Chandrarao More in his court, seated on a platform, flanked by Maratha retainers

dialogue.text: Javali belonged to Chandrarao More, an old Maratha house, loyal for generations to different overlords and now a feudatory of Bijapur, holding their valley as a jagir.

panels.shot: split composition: on one side Shivaji with his men; on the other, Chandrarao with his retainers, both looking toward the same mountains

dialogue.text: Both were Marathas. Both spoke the same tongue, worshipped at the same shrines, and yet their ambitions ran into each other in the stone ribs of the Ghats.

panels.shot: close-up on Shivaji’s face bent over documents and letters by lamplight

dialogue.text: Historians see the Deccan then as a world of mobile service elites, forever shifting between masters. Shivaji chose a harder path: to build authority rooted in land, forts and local support.

panels.shot: wide shot of caravan route descending from plateau, guarded by More’s men

dialogue.text: Control of Javali meant more than one fort. It meant tolls, safe passage for trade, and the narrow staircases by which armies could descend to the salt-smelling Konkan.

panels.shot: medium shot of Shivaji conferring with key lieutenants in an open courtyard

dialogue.text: For Shivaji, seizing Javali would link his hill kingdom to the Konkan, bring new revenues, and threaten Bijapur’s hold on the coast. But it also meant striking first at a fellow Maratha.

panels.shot: medium shot of Chandrarao More with a Bijapur emissary, exchanging formal courtesies

dialogue.text: Chandrarao, too, balanced worlds: answering to Bijapur for revenue and loyalty, yet ruling his valley with old hereditary authority. Each new power in the hills was a threat to that balance.

panels.shot: dynamic tracking shot of Shivaji’s small force moving stealthily through forest paths

dialogue.text: In 1656, Shivaji moved. Sources agree that his forces entered the Javali country with speed, guided by men who knew every ravine and rock of the valley.

panels.shot: wide shot of a More-held fort bracing for attack, defenders rushing to battlements

dialogue.text: The Bakhar chronicles speak of strong resistance. More’s forts did not fall to mere rumour. They had to be tested by siege and fear.

panels.shot: low-angle shot from behind Shivaji as he surveys a besieged fort from a nearby ridge

dialogue.text: Later Maratha narrators may embellish, but the outline is clear: forts were stormed or surrendered, Javali’s defenses strained, and Shivaji personally oversaw the tightening noose.

panels.shot: tense mid-shot hinting at a parley: two camps facing each other across a small clearing

dialogue.text: How Chandrarao himself met his end is disputed. Some Bakhars tell of a treacherous killing at parley; others imply death in battle. Modern historians leave the exact manner unresolved.

panels.shot: somber wide shot of the More household leaving with few belongings, watched by Shivaji’s officials

dialogue.text: What is clear is that Chandrarao’s power was broken. His lands, forts and revenues were absorbed. His household faded as Shivaji’s officials took charge of Javali.

panels.shot: medium shot of Shivaji receiving the keys of a fort from a local patil, with villagers watching

dialogue.text: Shivaji moved quickly to bind the valley. He confirmed some local chiefs, replaced others, and began weaving Javali into his growing network of forts, tax-collectors and village alliances.

panels.shot: epic bird’s-eye shot from high above Javali, a faint trail winding down toward the sparkling Konkan sea

dialogue.text: With Javali came a prize no enemy wanted him to hold: secure access to Konkan. Now hill-forts, coastal ports and inland markets could speak to each other under his banner.

panels.shot: interior shot of Bijapur court, nobles reacting as news is read aloud

dialogue.text: For Bijapur, this was no minor quarrel between Maratha feudatories. The loss of Javali signaled a bold hill chief seizing jagirs, defying the sultan, and linking plateau and sea under his own hand.

panels.shot: medium shot suggestion of Afzal Khan preparing in Bijapur, seen from behind as he dons armor

dialogue.text: Within a few years, Bijapur would send Afzal Khan against Shivaji, an escalation shaped not only by raids on Muslim jagirs, but by the memory of how a Maratha rival like More had been swept aside.

panels.shot: quiet medium shot of Shivaji standing alone on a cliff at dusk, looking toward Javali and the coast

dialogue.text: Victory in Javali was not over a foreign empire, but over a neighbour who shared his language and gods. The road to Swarajya was laid as much over such rivalries as over battles with distant sultans.
